prize_parts.citation: for the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, in which ligand design made the formation of aryl amines a general reaction

statement.case_for: My round-1 position stands: B011 alone, Buchwald and Hartwig. Having read all eight statements and put the chair's own first question to myself, my one-sentence answer on novelty is this. Heck, Negishi and Suzuki made C-C bonds through transmetalation of a carbon nucleophile; C-N coupling required a different catalytic cycle, in which amine binding, deprotonation and C-N reductive elimination from a Pd-amido complex are the hard steps, and it was only solved when ligand design (bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines on one side, hindered trialkyl and ferrocenyl phosphines on the other) lowered that barrier. That is a new mechanistic problem solved by a new design principle, not a new partner in an old reaction, and the citation should say carbon-nitrogen bond formation and ligand design so that it cannot be read as a repeat of 2010. Four members prefer it, all with the same two names and near-identical wording, and nobody argues that it is immature. It is the only shortlisted case with a clean two-name credit, more than 25 years of independent confirmation and a consequence that can be checked in the literature and in process chemistry. Kosugi belongs in the narrative: his tin-amide coupling showed Pd could join an amine and an aryl halide, but it was stoichiometric in tin and limited in scope, and the general catalytic method came from the later work.
statement.case_against: The 2010 overlap is a real objection, and a committee that regards C-N coupling as a late extension of a prize already given could reasonably decline. I also have not been given evidence that the tin-amide reaction was closer to the general method than I describe, so my Kosugi position rests on the descriptions in the files and not on a priority audit. Finally, B068 has the broadest ranking and is a field that is still opening; if the committee weights generative potential over maturity and clean credit, it has a legitimate claim, and I hold B011 partly because it can be defended without waiting for a clinical outcome, not because B068 is weaker science.

responses.point: Chabes prefers B068 (Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli), argues that the chemistry rather than the clinic must be mature, and notes that independent groups have reproduced and extended degraders for two decades.
responses.response: I accept that maturity of the chemistry, and not an approved drug, is the right test, and that changes how I weigh the missing approval: I no longer treat it as a reason to defer on its own. My remaining objection is the one you raise yourself in your case against: the PROTAC strand and the cereblon molecular-glue strand look to me like two discoveries with different logics, and three names cannot honour both. If the citation covers only bifunctional degraders, Handa's contribution is excluded from the prize it helped explain; if it covers both, the three names do not match the claim. Ciulli is the more defensible third name only if the committee limits the citation to designed bifunctional molecules, and I am not convinced the committee has settled that, and that is why I keep B068 as my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Aili prefers B068 (Crews, Deshaies, Handa), calls it the only candidate that founded a design principle and spread across fields, and concedes that credit is fragmented and the support is broad but shallow.
responses.response: I agree with your own assessment that the support is broad and shallow, and I think that is the decisive observation for a vote that needs five. Five of the seven opening ranks for B068 are third, fourth or eighth, and the round-1 statements show three of the members who ranked it do not prefer it. You asked what the citation sentence would be, and I put the same question to you: a sentence that covers a heterobifunctional design (Crews, Deshaies) and a monovalent glue discovered through thalidomide biology (Handa) in one clause is the thing I have not seen. If you can supply it, and show it is not two prizes in one, I would move B068 above my alternative position; until then I judge it a strong candidate that has not yet found its citation.

responses.point: Zou pairs B011 with a second part for nitrogenase structure (B003, Rees alone), to give two distinct, mature achievements within the three-person limit.
responses.response: I considered whether a two-part prize improves on B011 alone, and I do not support it. The nitrogenase part would credit Rees alone, which you yourself note leaves out Einsle, who solved the carbide-containing cofactor at high resolution, and Seefeldt, Dean and Ribbe, who built the biochemistry; and a part whose citation rests on structure while the N2-binding site and the cycle are unresolved is a weaker half than the first. Adding it would also spend the three-person limit on a lopsided 2+1 split to buy a second achievement that only you and Brzezinski rank. I would rather the committee sign a clean two-name B011 citation than a configuration whose second part invites the same attribution dispute we are trying to avoid.

responses.point: Sparr prefers B019 (Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen), holds that the same maturity yardstick should be applied to condensates as to PROTACs, and concedes that physiological relevance is contested and credit cannot be cut cleanly at three.
responses.response: You are right that I should apply one yardstick, and I do: by it B019 is the younger and less settled of the two, and your own case against says the functional significance of the material state is unresolved and that the natural home may be physiology. I credit the 2009 P-granule droplet result and the phase-diagram framework as real concepts, but I still cannot name observations in cells that are beyond dispute, and the fourth and fifth names (Pappu, Mittag) show the credit does not stop at three. I therefore leave B019 off my list; I would revisit it in a later year if the in-cell evidence consolidates.

responses.point: Somfai prefers B011 alone, argues the evidence of adoption can be read in the literature, and grants that B068 has broader support and is a newer modality.
responses.response: I agree with your reading and I am grateful for the point about adoption that can be checked in the literature, since it is the strongest answer to the 2010 objection. I would add one thing the committee should settle before the vote: that the citation names C-N bond formation and ligand design explicitly, as you did, so that the novelty relative to Heck, Negishi and Suzuki is on the page and not left to a speaker's explanation. On Kosugi I take the same position as you, credit in the background and not in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee as a whole regards C-N coupling as distinct from the 2010 prize; the supporters of B011 are four of eight and need a fifth.
Whether Kosugi's precursor deserves any place beyond the narrative; I have seen no evidence that it was general or catalytic in the later sense.
Whether B068 can be given a single citation and three names that cover both PROTACs and molecular glues, and whether that happens this year.
Whether my own shift from B039 in round 1 reflects the evidence or the pull of the room, which I try to guard against by stating the mechanistic case on its merits.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I am a Lund physicist and colleague of Somfai and Sparr, and chair; I have no stated personal or institutional link to Buchwald, Hartwig, Kosugi or the PROTAC, sequencing or phase-separation candidates. My field proximity to molecular motors does not bear on any shortlisted part.
